content: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is a condition that affects approximately 1.9 out of every 1000 newborns. The incidence may be higher in developing countries. There is robust evidence supporting the use of inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as effective treatments for PPHN. However, these therapies are expensive and require advanced technical expertise, which may not be available in many developing regions. Magnesium sulfate is known to be a potent vasodilator, meaning it can relax and widen blood vessels. This property suggests that it may have the potential to lower the elevated pulmonary arterial pressures seen in PPHN. If magnesium sulfate proves to be effective in treating PPHN, it could serve as a cost-effective and potentially life-saving alternative to more expensive therapies like iNO and ECMO. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of magnesium sulfate compared to placebo, standard ventilator management alone, sildenafil infusion, adenosine infusion, or inhaled nitric oxide. The primary outcomes of interest were mortality rates and the need for backup therapies such as iNO or ECMO in term and near-term newborns (greater than 34 weeks of gestational age) diagnosed with PPHN. To identify relevant studies, the researchers employed the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group (CNRG). No restrictions were placed on language. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library, Issue 1, 2006) and MEDLINE (from 1966 to April 20, 2007) were searched. Additionally, reference lists of retrieved articles were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to obtain any unpublished data. The search was updated in December 2009. The inclusion criteria for the review required randomized or quasi-randomized studies in which one of the treatment groups received magnesium sulfate for PPHN. Standard Cochrane Collaboration and CNRG methods were used for data collection and analysis. This included independent assessments of trial quality and data extraction by each author. The main finding of the review was that no eligible trials were identified. As a result, there is currently no evidence to support the use of magnesium sulfate in the treatment of PPHN. The authors concluded that, based on the lack of available evidence, magnesium sulfate cannot be recommended for this purpose. They emphasized the need for randomized controlled trials to evaluate its efficacy and safety in this context.
